GOLDMAN SACHS
SUMMER ANALYST INTERVIEW EXPERIENCE
YEAR - 2024
MANAV SHAH
COMPUTER ENGINEERING
BATCH - 2026

Introduction
Hey there, I am Manav Shah, a BTech CE student of VJTI (2023 - 2026). I would like to
share my interview experience for the Goldman Sachs Internship opportunity as a
Summer Analyst. I hope my experience will help you prepare better for both
internship and FTE (Full-Time Employment) opportunities at Goldman Sachs.
The selection process included three interview rounds and an online assessment.
Each stage was crucial in assessing various skills, such as technical knowledge,
problem-solving abilities, and communication. I will share as many details as I
remember from my experience, hoping it will give you valuable insights and guide
your preparation effectively.
Pre Placement Talk
Somewhere around 12 July 2024, we received an email from TPO informing us that
Goldman Sachs was visiting the campus for intern hiring. In this email, there were
links for applying on the official Goldman Sachs Careers page as well as details for a
webinar.
Platform: Zoom Webinar.
Time: 23 July 2024, 5pm - 6pm.
The Pre-Placement Talk was engaging and to the point. They started off by
explaining what GS does, why GS stands out from the rest and what kind of lifestyle
you can expect at GS.
Pay close attention to whatever is discussed in this meeting, as it serves as a good
way to understand the kind of people the firm is looking for. Additionally, during your
interviews, the interviewers may ask you questions about the firm, and the insights
shared in this session can help you make a strong impression. Preparing for this talk
and taking detailed notes will definitely pay off in the later stages of the hiring
process.
2

Online Assessment (OA)
Platform - Hackerank (Video and Screen proctored)
Duration - Around 1 hour
The online assessment consisted of:
●
10 multiple-choice questions (MCQs) -15 mins
●
3 coding questions - 40 mins
●
1 HR-related questions - 5mins
As much as I remember, we were allocated 55 minutes to complete the MCQs and
coding questions, and an additional 5 minutes for the HR questions. Each MCQ earns
you 3 marks for correct answer and -1 mark for incorrect answer.
Coding Questions - 3 Questions
1) Modest Number
The problem is to identify modest numbers within a given range (inclusive of start
and end). A number is considered modest if it can be split into two parts (left and
right), such that dividing the number by the right part gives a remainder equal to the
left part. The program should check all possible combinations of left and right
partitions of a number to verify this condition.
Solution Approach
1.
Splitting Numbers: Iterate over all digits of a number to partition it into left and
right parts.
2.
Validation: Check if the right part is non-zero and if the condition number %
right == left holds.
3.
Iterate Over Range: For every number in the given range, apply the above
check.
3

4. Output: Collect and print all numbers that satisfy the modest number
property.
This approach ensures all possible partitions are tested for each number within the
range.
2) Identifying Unique Colors on Painting Sheets
Problem:
You are given N rectangular painting sheets and M shots. Each sheet is defined by
four integers representing the bottom-left and top-right corners of the rectangle, i.e.,
(x1, y1) and (x2, y2). Each shot has a set of coordinates (x, y) and a color. The goal is to
determine, for each sheet, how many unique colors have been shot within the
boundaries of that sheet.
●
For each shot, you need to check if the shot's coordinates lie within the bounds
of each painting sheet.
●
If the shot is within a sheet, the color of that shot should be considered for that
sheet.
Input:
●
N (number of painting sheets) and M (number of shots).
●
N rectangles, each defined by four integers (x1, y1, x2, y2), representing the
coordinates of the bottom-left and top-right corners.
●
M shots, each defined by three integers: (x, y) for the coordinates and color
for the color of the shot.
Output:
●
For each sheet, output the number of unique colors that have been shot within
the sheet's bounds.
4

Solution Approach:
1.
Store Sheet Data: Each sheet is represented by a rectangle with four
coordinates (x1, y1, x2, y2).
2.
Track Unique Colors: For each shot, check if the shot’s coordinates fall within
the bounds of each sheet. If they do, add the color of the shot to the respective
sheet's set.
3.
Output: After processing all shots, the size of each sheet’s set will give the
number of unique colors associated with that sheet.
This approach efficiently uses sets to ensure that only unique colors are counted for
each sheet.
3) Card
The problem involved using a greedy approach and working with arrays. While I
can't recall the exact details of the question, it revolved around distributing or sorting
cards in some way that required an optimal solution using a greedy strategy. The
task likely involved finding a way to minimize or maximize certain values based on
the cards' properties (such as their values, positions, or some other attributes).
MCQs - 10 Questions
1.
Blocks of Different Colours Flock Together: This problem involves calculating
the probability of selecting three balls of different colors from a box containing
white, black, and red balls, given certain relationships between the number of
balls of each color.
2.
Printer and Bookshelf Efficiency: This scenario involves a printer and a
bookshelf with various operations like printing papers, stacking books, and
handling failures (paper getting stuck or books falling down), represented by
different operations (X, Y, Z, W).
3.
Binary Tree Check: This question is about the properties of a complete binary
tree, where you need to identify the correct statement related to the structure
and characteristics of a complete binary tree.
5

4. Reality TV: In this problem, you're asked to calculate the number of ways to
form a group of six people from eight teams, ensuring that exactly one team's
both members are selected.
5. Probability Games: This question involves selecting three balls from a box
containing prime numbers from 1 to 30 and finding the probability that the
sum of their numbers is even and their product is less than 500.
6. Sequence Check: This problem asks you to verify or identify properties of a
given sequence of numbers or elements.
7.
Binary
Tree
Nodes:
This
question
likely
asks
about
the
properties
or
characteristics related to the number of nodes in a binary tree and how they
are structured.
8. Multiple
Inheritance:
This
question
tests
knowledge
about
multiple
inheritance in object-oriented programming, particularly in terms of how it
works and the challenges associated with it.
9. Queue-Stack Time: This question is about analyzing the time complexity of
insertions and deletions in a queue, given a specific number of push and pop
operations.
10. Linked List: This problem involves operations on a linked list, testing knowledge
of how linked lists function and the operations that can be performed on them.
HR Question - 1 Question
The question was how I would ensure a smooth transition of responsibilities if I were
leaving a team. Specifically, the question was: "If you are leaving a team, how will you
make sure you communicate all the important details and responsibilities to another
team member?" The focus was on how to effectively transfer knowledge and tasks to
ensure the continuity of the team's work.
Results:
27 people were shortlisted for interviews, and I was one of them. We received the
results on 25 July 2024, in the afternoon.
6

Interview Day
Date: 26 July 2024
Venue: TPO Seminar Hall
The day started with a reporting time of 8:30 am, followed by the Pre-Interview Talk
scheduled at 9:00 am. We were instructed to bring 3-4 printouts of our resumes and
dress formally. I wore a white shirt, black trousers, a belt, and formal shoes. Dressing
well is crucial, especially when interviewing with financial firms, so make sure to
present yourself professionally.
A team of around 6-7 people from GS was responsible for managing the process.
About five of them were engineers from GS, while the rest were HR/Managerial
personnel. During the Pre-Interview Talk, they gave us an overview of the interview
procedure and their roles at GS. They explained that the interview would consist of
technical rounds followed by HR rounds.
After the talk, the interview process began around 10 am without any delays.
A few important tips to keep in mind before the interview:
1.
Pay attention to the Pre-Interview Talk: Focus on the introductions and the
roles of the people from GS. This knowledge might be useful, as you may end
up with one of them as your interviewer.
2.
Engage with the questions: If there's a Q&A session or any general questions
are asked, make sure to answer. Most candidates tend to stay silent, so
responding will make you stand out.
3.
Ask about the company: Show your interest by asking questions regarding the
technologies the company is working on or other relevant aspects of the
organization.
4. Research the company: Before the interview, make sure to gather background
details about the company, including its latest news and collaborations. This
will help you stand out as an informed candidate and show your genuine
interest.
7

Round 1: Technical Interview (Duration: 1 hr)
The interviews began at 10 am, but my first technical round didn’t start until 12 pm,
which was quite nerve-wracking, especially since some candidates had already
completed two rounds by that time.
The TPO seminar hall had several cabins, each with one or two interviewers, and
candidates were allocated to different cabins. Finally, I was called for my first
technical interview. I sat down across from my interviewer, who introduced himself
and explained his role at GS. He then asked me to introduce myself. I gave my
introduction confidently. It’s important to have a well-prepared introduction—keep it
concise and to the point. Avoid going too technical and consider mentioning a
hobby or an interesting fact. Remember to maintain good eye contact and positive
body language.
Then after asking me which language I was comfortable with(C++), he gave me the
1st question and a piece of pen and paper to solve it on.
1.
Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
Given a binary tree root, a node X in the tree is named good if in the path from
root to X there are no nodes with a value greater than X.
Return the number of good nodes in the binary tree.
Input: root = [3,1,4,3,null,1,5]
Output: 4
Explanation: Nodes in blue are good.
Root Node (3) is always a good node.
8

Node 4 -> (3,4) is the maximum value in the path starting from the root.
Node 5 -> (3,4,5) is the maximum value in the path
Node 3 -> (3,1,3) is the maximum value in the path.
It was an easy question, and I explained my approach to the interviewer before
writing any code. I described how I would solve it using Depth-First Search (DFS) to
traverse the tree and keep track of the largest value encountered in the path from
the root to each node. I also mentioned that for a node to be considered "good," its
value must be greater than or equal to the largest value in the path from the root to
that node.
Here’s the approach I explained to the interviewer:
●
Perform a DFS traversal on the tree to visit each node.
●
At each node, compare its value with the largest value encountered so far
(curMax).
●
If the node’s value is greater than or equal to curMax, increment the count of
good nodes.
●
Recursively traverse the left and right subtrees, passing the updated curMax
value.
Additional Tips:
●
Always mention the time and space complexity even if the interviewer doesn't
ask.
●
Use proper variable naming conventions to make your code more readable
and maintainable.
●
Consider various edge cases and test your code against them. Running your
code on different test cases impresses the interviewer as it shows thorough
thinking and problem-solving skills.
9

2. Design a Gmail System
The second question in my technical round was quite unique and interesting. The
task was to design a mail system with various features and operations. The mail
system needed to support the following components:
1.
Unread: Stores emails that have not yet been read.
2.
Read: Stores emails that have been read.
3.
Spam: Stores emails that are marked as spam.
4. Deleted: Stores emails that have been deleted.
Additionally, there were various operations to perform on the emails:
1.
X: Marks email X as "read" and moves it from the "Unread" queue to the "Read"
queue.
2.
X: Marks email X as "spam" and moves it from either the "Read" or "Unread"
queue to the "Spam" queue.
3.
X: Moves email X from the "Spam" queue back to the "Unread" queue.
4. X: Deletes email X from the system and add it to delete queue.
10

Approach:
I started by explaining to the interviewer that we could maintain separate queues for
each component: "Read", "Unread", "Spam", and "Deleted".
●
When we receive an email (let's say X), it will first be placed in the "Unread"
queue.
●
When the user performs an operation like "read", the mail X is moved from
"Unread" to "Read".
●
Similarly, other operations can move emails between queues while
maintaining the FIFO property of each queue.
This was the basic approach I outlined, and the interviewer was satisfied with it. Then,
he asked me about the time complexity of the solution. I explained that each
operation would take O(n) time because we would need to traverse the entire queue
to find the email, remove it from the old queue, and add it to the new queue.
Optimization:
The interviewer then asked me to reduce the time complexity from O(n) to O(1) per
operation. Initially, I struggled to think of how to achieve this, but after a while, I
brainstormed different data structures. He provided me with a hint about using
linear data structures.
Eventually, I realized that I could use a Doubly Linked List to store the nodes and
maps to track the positions of emails. Specifically, I proposed using a map like <mail,
Node>* to directly locate any email in O(1) time. This way, we could:
●
Remove an email from a queue in O(1) time by modifying the left and right
pointers of its adjacent nodes.
●
Add it to another queue in O(1) time by adjusting the pointers.
This solution is quite similar to how LRU (Least Recently Used) cache and LFU (Least
Frequently Used) cache work and I had already solved those while practicing.
11

Since the code would be large and we were under time constraints, the interviewer
asked me to design the map structures and explain the workflow of the operations
rather than writing the full code.
Outcome:
The interviewer was impressed with this approach, as it was a novel solution to a
unique and challenging problem.
3. Count Unique Occurrences of Different Characters in a String
The third question I was asked was to count the unique occurrences of different
characters in a string. This was a relatively straightforward question.
Approach:
I started by explaining to the interviewer that the problem could be solved by
maintaining a map (or a hash map) to store the frequency of each character in the
string. After iterating through the string, we could check the frequency of each
character and track the unique occurrences.
Here’s the basic approach I described:
●
Traverse the string and maintain a map to store the frequency of each
character.
●
After processing the string, count how many characters have unique
frequencies.
This was an easy problem to solve, and I told the interviewer the time complexity and
space complexity:
Time Complexity:
Since we only need to iterate over the string once, the time complexity is O(n), where
n is the length of the string.
Space Complexity:
The space complexity is O(1), as there are at most limited different characters in the
12

string . This makes the space complexity constant because the number of different
characters is fixed.
The interviewer seemed satisfied with my approach and explanation.
I was selected for the second round.
Round 2: Technical + Design (Duration: 40 mins)
I was selected for the second round, which was a combination of Technical and
Design. The round began with the interviewer asking me to introduce myself. I gave a
brief, clear, and concise introduction, after which the interviewer reviewed my
resume. She then asked me about the different blockchain projects I had worked on,
requesting more detailed information about each one. Following that, she asked
about my previous internship experience, and we discussed it in detail.
After this, the interviewer transitioned to the design portion of the round. She asked
me to design a high-level architecture for a company with multiple departments.
Each department had both common features and unique features specific to that
department. I was tasked with designing a system to accommodate this scenario.
I started by asking a few clarifying questions to ensure I understood all aspects of the
problem and then proceeded to design the solution on paper. My approach was to
create a Company class and then Department classes that would inherit from the
main class. Each department class would inherit common features and have
additional unique features specific to that department.
For common features, I suggested creating a separate class that would house all
the shared features, ensuring code reusability. Each department class would then
extend this common class and add its own unique attributes and functionalities.
13

When the interviewer asked which OOP concepts I would use for this design, I
mentioned
inheritance
and
encapsulation.
She
then

which
type

inheritance I would use, and I initially said multiple inheritance. The interviewer
pointed out that Java does not support multiple inheritance, but I quickly adapted
and explained that interfaces could be used as an alternative in Java to achieve the
desired functionality.
She then asked how I would implement this system in React. I explained that I would
create modular code using different components, ensuring code reusability across
the application.
The conversation shifted, and the interviewer asked me a random question related
to streaming services. She asked, "When you watch a movie on Netflix and click on
14

‘continue watching,’ it starts from where you last left off. But in Zee5, it starts a few
seconds before that point. What do you think is the reason for this difference?"
I thought for a moment and suggested that Zee5 might be dividing the video into
fixed frames and resuming from the nearest previous frame. The interviewer
confirmed my answer for Zee5 but clarified that Netflix uses a sliding window data
structure to handle this functionality. I was a bit surprised by this and was curious
about how this data structure is implemented.
After this, the interviewer asked me if I had any questions. I asked about the reason
behind GS migrating from a private cloud to AWS (a public cloud) and how they
manage to send years of data to AWS. She answered my query, and that concluded
my second round.
I was selected for the third round.
Round 3 : HR Round (Duration: 25 - 30 minutes)
The HR round began with a question about why I chose to join VJTI and what
motivated me. I shared my entire journey, explaining how VJTI was the ideal place for
my academic and professional growth.
The interviewer then noticed some blockchain projects listed on my resume and
asked me about the scope and future of blockchain technology. He also inquired
about my experience in participating in hackathons. I elaborated on the potential
and future growth of blockchain and how hackathons have sharpened my skills and
encouraged innovation.
Next, the interviewer presented a practical scenario regarding the IRCTC app. He
asked about a situation where millions of people are trying to book tickets
simultaneously, but only 100 seats are available. He wanted to know why it takes
seven working days for refunds to be processed and whether the government uses
this money for their own profit. After a brief pause, I explained that the government
likely doesn’t use the funds for profit. Since different people have bank accounts in
various banks, and the government maintains the money in a single account, the
15

refund process involves transferring funds to multiple accounts, which takes time. He
seemed satisfied with my response.
He then asked how IRCTC would allocate a single seat when hundreds of people are
competing for it. I explained that since the booking happens in microseconds, the
system would differentiate based on time and other factors like age, gender, and
priority. The seat would be allocated accordingly. We discussed this in more detail.
The interviewer then asked me a thought-provoking question on how to prevent fake
messages from being circulated on social media platforms like WhatsApp. I initially
suggested that a machine learning model could be developed, which would be
trained on verified news data to classify messages as fake or legitimate. The idea
was that the model would learn patterns, language cues, and credibility indicators
from trusted sources, allowing it to effectively flag false information.
However, the interviewer raised an important point: there is no readily available
dataset to train such a model, especially for a platform like WhatsApp, where
messages are often private and shared informally. This posed a challenge, but I
quickly adapted and proposed an alternative approach. I suggested that instead of
relying
solely
on
a
machine
learning
model,
we
could
implement
a
community-driven reporting system. In this system, users would be able to flag
messages they believe to be fake. Once a message is reported by multiple users, the
system could mark it as potentially false, prompting further verification or action. This
crowdsourced approach would leverage the collective input of the platform’s users
to help identify and combat fake news in real-time.
Finally, I asked several questions about the work culture at GS and how the company
competes with other banks that are introducing new technologies. The interviewer
gave detailed answers, which concluded the HR round.
16

Result:
After my interview, I returned to the TPO hall, feeling a lot more relaxed now that it
was over. I sat down with my friends who had also finished their interviews, and we
chatted until around 6 pm. At that point, the team from Goldman Sachs came in and
announced that they would be declaring the results on the spot.
The HR manager came in with a stack of around six resumes and began reading the
names, one by one, in alphabetical order. As each name was called, the tension in
the room grew. My heart started racing when I realized my name hadn’t come up yet.
Towards the end, I noticed that the last resume was in her hand, and I couldn’t help
but feel a bit nervous. Finally, she called out “Manav Shah.” .They selected six people
and I was one of them.
It was a strange mix of relief and surprise. I exchanged congratulations with the
others, but I also felt a bit sad as I noticed some of my friends weren't selected. It’s
always tough when others don’t make it, but I knew that’s how interviews work—some
get selected, and some don’t.
Once I stepped outside, I immediately called my parents. They were so relieved and
proud of my efforts, and their support made the moment even more special. It felt
great knowing they were happy with my hard work paying off.
Key takeaways:
1.
Building a strong resume is crucial, and it’s important to focus only on the skills
and technologies you’re truly comfortable with. Don’t forget to seek feedback
from seniors to make improvements, and try to increase your ATS score to
enhance your chances of getting shortlisted.
2.
During interviews, it’s essential to communicate your thought process clearly.
Speaking out loud while solving problems not only helps interviewers follow
your logic but also gives them the opportunity to provide hints if you're
heading in the wrong direction. It’s equally important to mention edge cases
17

during problem-solving, as it shows your thorough approach to tackling
challenges.
3.
Make sure to practice core computer science concepts like DSA, OOPS, and
DBMS regularly. Companies may begin their recruitment process during
vacations, so being consistently prepared will give you an advantage. Also,
stay on top of CS fundamentals to ensure you’re ready when the opportunity
arises.
4. While technical skills are a must, how you express them matters just as much.
When you’re unsure or nervous, take a deep breath, and don’t hesitate to ask
the interviewer for clarification. It demonstrates that you’re thinking critically
before answering, rather than rushing.
5. At CoC, we have mock interviews conducted by seniors, which were incredibly
helpful for practicing and receiving constructive feedback before facing the
real deal. These mock sessions gave me a chance to refine my skills in a more
relaxed environment.
6. Lastly, reading through other candidates’ interview experiences can provide
valuable insights, as interview formats are often similar across companies.
This will help you better understand what to expect and how to approach
different interview stages.
Preparation Tips
1.
Take part in LeetCode contests to sharpen your problem-solving speed, and
try solving the "LeetCode Daily Question" each day for consistent practice.
2.
Review core Computer Science fundamentals, including Operating Systems
(OS), Object-Oriented Programming (OOPS), and Database Management
Systems
(DBMS).
If
time
allows,
explore
Computer
Networks
(CN)
and
low/high-level design concepts.
3.
Focus on key interview questions related to your preferred programming
language. For instance, for Java, check relevant resources for common
interview questions.
4. Prepare a strong self-introduction and familiarize yourself with behavioral
questions that typically come up in HR rounds.
18

5. Know your resume inside out. Be ready to answer questions about the
technologies used in your projects, such as Firebase, MongoDB, React, etc., by
reviewing sources like InterviewBit or GeeksforGeeks (GFG).
6. Understand your projects thoroughly and use the STAR method (Situation,
Task, Action, Result) to explain your contributions, especially for team projects.
7.
There are countless resources available, but don’t get overwhelmed. Start your
preparation with the materials that resonate with your learning style and
make sense to you.
8. Commit to solving at least one or two problems daily to maintain a steady
pace and avoid falling behind. Staying consistent is key.
9. Go through past interview experiences, as they can offer valuable insights into
the interview format and types of questions asked.
10. Discuss
problems
and
approaches with friends or peers to learn new
techniques and discover questions or methods you may not have considered.
11. Avoid comparing your progress with others. Focus on your personal growth
and trust the preparation process that works best for you.

Conclusion
To sum up, the most important takeaway is from the points mentioned earlier. If you
don’t get selected, don’t let it discourage you. Interviews are a mix of skill and
luck—around 50% luck and 50% skill. The interviewer's mood, their preferences, and
the other candidates are all factors beyond your control, so don’t be disheartened by
a rejection. Take it as a learning experience, and know that things will eventually fall
into place. For instance, my friend interviewed with 7-8 companies with 14-15
interviews before finally landing an offer, so persistence is key.
If you do get selected, take the time to celebrate your achievement! It’s not easy, and
it takes hard work to reach this point. Afterward, take a break and enjoy the moment,
then offer your support to friends who are still preparing. Help them by conducting
mock interviews to give back.
With this I will end my interview experience here, I hope you never felt boring
throughout the interview experience.
If you have any questions regarding my GS interview experience or need advice on
interview preparation, feel free to reach out to me at manavshah1104@gmail.com.
I’ll be happy to help as soon as I can.
ALL THE BEST !!!
